Consider the matrix $P$ shown above. Given that $A=PDP^T$ is an orthogonal diagonalization of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ for some diagonal matrix $D,$ which of the following could be the first column of the matrix $P?$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14075254/assets/18abb9c5165a3fe54a0f3067cf5325bfd4bd0fa4243c841ce4e7bb95c25dddda.png)
e-8157.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PDP^T,
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix.

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

Since  $A=PDP^T$ is an orthogonal diagonalization of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A,$ the matrix $P$ must be a $2\times 2$ orthogonal matrix. This means that 

- the first column must be orthogonal to the second column, and

- the norm of the first column must be equal to $1.$

Among the given options, only the vector $[\begin{aligned}\frac{3\sqrt{10}}{10} \\ -\frac{\sqrt{10}}{10}\end{aligned}]$ has both properties.

Consider the matrices shown above. 
Given that $D=P^T \! AP,$ where $P$ is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the first column of the matrix $P?$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14075254/assets/9acec021ce321e77ad541ecbb0a38944aa4991ec26c721e0e59a521490269d06.png)
e-8164.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PDP^T,
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

$$
D=P^TAP.
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that $A$ is symmetric and $D$ is diagonal. Therefore, $D=P^T \! AP$ gives an orthogonal diagonalization of $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are $\lambda_1=-1$ and $\lambda_2=1.$ So, the first column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda_1=-1.$ 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda_1=-1.$ Computing $A-(-1)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A+I & =[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ -1 & 0\end{aligned}]+[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, $x_2$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain $x_1=x_2.$ Hence, the general solution is

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14075254/assets/efb691aec933aa631974add9dc9d7d122b03f5956b17459eb0e76751e07ea42a.png)

Therefore, setting $x_2=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14075254/assets/8c0ac2201e3e40bcc8e5e71c12413504694b201237069a4695fae94d33e7fcb4.png)

where $\| \mathbf{v}_1 \| = \sqrt{2}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm, we obtain the first column of $P\mathbin{:}$ 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14075254/assets/1490159efc1ac2073ee029f918c136b7c16fd77b5f15e59334a3ae63e08a8c92.png)

decision.explanation: P must have orthonormal columns. Option b is perpendicular to the first column because (12/13)(5/13)+(5/13)(-12/13)=0. Its squared norm is (25+144)/169=1, so it is a valid second column.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem:
$$
P=[\begin{aligned}\frac{12}{13} & \,∗\, \\ \frac{5}{13} & \,∗\,\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrix $P$ shown above. Given that $A=PD{P}^{T}$ is an orthogonal diagonalization of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ for some diagonal matrix $D,$ which of the following could be the second column of the matrix $P?$
after.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix.

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

Since  $A=PD{P}^{T}$ is an orthogonal diagonalization of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A,$ the matrix $P$ must be a $2\times 2$ orthogonal matrix. This means that 

- the second column must be orthogonal to the first column, and

- the norm of the second column must be equal to $1.$

Among the given options, only the vector $[\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{13} \\ -\frac{12}{13}\end{aligned}]$ has both properties.

P=[1213∗513∗] Consider the matrix P shown above. Given that A=PDPT is an orthogonal diagonalization of a 2×2 symmetric matrix A for some diagonal matrix D, which of the following could be the second column of the matrix P?

a
[1213−513]
b
[513−1213]
c
[12−5]
d
[5−12]
e
[−513−1213]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Recall that a matrix A is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix P such that

A=PDPT, where D is a diagonal matrix.

Moreover, a matrix A is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

Since A=PDPT is an orthogonal diagonalization of a 2×2 symmetric matrix A, the matrix P must be a 2×2 orthogonal matrix. This means that

  • the second column must be orthogonal to the first column, and

  • the norm of the second column must be equal to 1.

Among the given options, only the vector [513−1213] has both properties.

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms b. Its dot product with the first column is (60-60)/169=0, and its squared norm is (25+144)/169=1. The observed incorrect submission selected a, not b.

content.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix.

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

Since  $A=PD{P}^{T}$ is an orthogonal diagonalization of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A,$ the matrix $P$ must be a $2\times 2$ orthogonal matrix. This means that 

- the second column must be orthogonal to the first column, and

- the norm of the second column must be equal to $1.$

Among the given options, only the vector $[\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{13} \\ -\frac{12}{13}\end{aligned}]$ has both properties.

after.name: Question 4
after.problem:
$$
P=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3} & \,∗\, \\ \frac{1}{3} & \,∗\,\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrix $P$ shown above. Given that $A=PD{P}^{T}$ is an orthogonal diagonalization of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ for some diagonal matrix $D,$ which of the following could be the second column of the matrix $P?$
after.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix.

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

Since  $A=PD{P}^{T}$ is an orthogonal diagonalization of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A,$ the matrix $P$ must be a $2\times 2$ orthogonal matrix. This means that 

- the second column must be orthogonal to the first column, and

- the norm of the second column must be equal to $1.$

Among the given options, only the vector $[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ -\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3}\end{aligned}]$ has both properties.

P=[223∗13∗] Consider the matrix P shown above. Given that A=PDPT is an orthogonal diagonalization of a 2×2 symmetric matrix A for some diagonal matrix D, which of the following could be the second column of the matrix P?

a

[22313]

[223−13]

[13−223]

Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Recall that a matrix A is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix P such that

A=PDPT, where D is a diagonal matrix.

Moreover, a matrix A is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

Since A=PDPT is an orthogonal diagonalization of a 2×2 symmetric matrix A, the matrix P must be a 2×2 orthogonal matrix. This means that

  • the second column must be orthogonal to the first column, and

  • the norm of the second column must be equal to 1.

Among the given options, only the vector [13−223] has both properties.

content.knowledge_point: Identifying Parts of an Orthogonal Diagonalization
content.problem:
$$
P=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3} & \,∗\, \\ \frac{1}{3} & \,∗\,\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrix $P$ shown above. Given that $A=PD{P}^{T}$ is an orthogonal diagonalization of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ for some diagonal matrix $D,$ which of the following could be the second column of the matrix $P?$
content.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix.

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

Since  $A=PD{P}^{T}$ is an orthogonal diagonalization of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A,$ the matrix $P$ must be a $2\times 2$ orthogonal matrix. This means that 

- the second column must be orthogonal to the first column, and

- the norm of the second column must be equal to $1.$

Among the given options, only the vector $[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \\ -\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{3}\end{aligned}]$ has both properties.

after.name: Question 5
after.problem:
$$
P=[\begin{aligned}\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{5} & \,∗\, \\ -\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5} & \,∗\,\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrix $P$ shown above. Given that $A=PD{P}^{T}$ is an orthogonal diagonalization of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A$ for some diagonal matrix $D,$ which of the following could be the second column of the matrix $P?$
after.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix.

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

Since  $A=PD{P}^{T}$ is an orthogonal diagonalization of a $2\times 2$ symmetric matrix $A,$ the matrix $P$ must be a $2\times 2$ orthogonal matrix. This means that 

- the second column must be orthogonal to the first column, and

- the norm of the second column must be equal to $1.$

Among the given options, only the vector $[\begin{aligned}\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5} \\ \frac{2\sqrt{5}}{5}\end{aligned}]$ has both properties.

after.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 4 \\ 4 & 4\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. 
Given that $D={P}^{T}\,AP,$ where $P$ is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the first column of the matrix $P.$
after.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

$$
D={P}^{T}AP.
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that $A$ is symmetric and $D$ is diagonal. Therefore, $D={P}^{T}\,AP$ gives an orthogonal diagonalization of $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=6.$ So, the first column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-4.$ 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{1}=-4.$ Computing $A-(-4)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A+4I & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 4 \\ 4 & 4\end{aligned}]+4[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 4 & 8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 4 & 8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 0 \\ 4 & 8 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-2{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

where $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{5}.$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm, we obtain the first column of $P:$ 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{5} \\ \frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}\end{aligned}]
$$

content.knowledge_point: Orthogonally Diagonalizing a 2x2 Symmetric Matrix Given Part of the Diagonalization
content.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 4 \\ 4 & 4\end{aligned}],\,D=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above. 
Given that $D={P}^{T}\,AP,$ where $P$ is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the first column of the matrix $P.$
content.worked_solution:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

$$
A=PD{P}^{T},
$$

where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

$$
D={P}^{T}AP.
$$

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that $A$ is symmetric and $D$ is diagonal. Therefore, $D={P}^{T}\,AP$ gives an orthogonal diagonalization of $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are ${\lambda }_{1}=-4$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=6.$ So, the first column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=-4.$ 

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to ${\lambda }_{1}=-4.$ Computing $A-(-4)I,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}A+4I & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 4 \\ 4 & 4\end{aligned}]+4[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 4 & 8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 4 & 8\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 0 \\ 4 & 8 & 0\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain ${x}_{1}=-2{x}_{2}.$ Hence, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}-2{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Therefore, setting ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector 

$$
{v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],
$$

where $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{5}.$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm, we obtain the first column of $P:$ 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{2\sqrt{5}}{5} \\ \frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}\end{aligned}]
$$
